blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Cooperative driving can extend a vehicle's awareness beyond its own sensors, but existing cooperative end-to-end methods inject shared information into the planner and rely on cooperative driving demonstrations to learn how to use it. The moments in which shared information should change a driving decision are rare in such data, providing limited supervision for learning this behavior. We argue that cooperation need not be learned by the planner. Instead, reacting to shared information requires predicting how surrounding agents will move and selecting a response from the candidate trajectories of an ego planner. We introduce CoSel, a cooperation-as-selection framework that leaves the planner and its ego-only input unchanged. A separately trained cooperative predictor uses observations from the ego vehicle, roadside units, and connected automated vehicles to predict surrounding agents and their future motion. CoSel evaluates the planner's candidate trajectories against these predictions, preserves the planner's choice when it remains safe, and selects the closest safe alternative when shared information reveals additional risk. Each safety intervention is traceable to the shared evidence that triggers it. In closed-loop evaluation, CoSel achieves a driving score of 70.7 on V2Xverse, outperforming the best compared cooperative method by 7.5 points, and the highest average driving score of 85.8 on MDrive. Under missing ego detections, the collision count of CoSel increases only from 17 to 19 in 72 scenarios, compared with 19 to 32 for an existing cooperative end-to-end model.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Cooperative driving extends a vehicle’s awareness with the perception [ 71 , 70 , 24 , 76 , 77 ] and intent [ 45 , 19 ] shared by roadside units (RSUs) and other connected automated vehicles
(CAVs).
A single vehicle, however good its end-to-end planner [ 59 , 51 ] , cannot obtain this information from
its own sensors: what lies behind an occluder, such as a pedestrian behind a kiosk ( Fig. 1 ), and what other
vehicles intend, as at an unsignalized intersection.

Existing cooperative end-to-end methods fuse the shared information into the planner, as raw data [ 75 ] or as
features or queries [ 46 , 78 , 57 ] , and train the planner on cooperative driving data.
Language-based methods instead pass shared messages to a large language
model [ 20 , 19 , 48 , 45 , 15 ] . In the fusion-based methods the perception that
feeds the planner can be supervised with labels, but how the planner uses it is learned from the expert’s trajectory.
The planner has to infer from imitation alone when shared information should change its decision.

This is hard to learn, because the frames that could teach it are rare. Imitation supervises a planner with
one ego trajectory per frame, a sparse signal [ 7 , 37 ] , and the frames in which the expert
changes its action because of an event in the scene, such as a light turning green or a pedestrian stepping out, are
a very small fraction [ 12 , 64 ] . As a result, a learned planner can reach a low
imitation error by continuing its own speed and past
motion [ 12 , 64 , 39 ] , and an additional input is not guaranteed to be
used correctly [ 17 ] . Of these frames, only a subset can teach the planner anything about shared
information: those in which the event is reported by an RSU or a CAV and is not visible to the ego’s own sensors. We
call these frames decision-changing moments : only in them should shared information change the decision. In
every other frame it adds little to what the ego already sees, and the demonstration gives no signal for using it.
In V2Xverse training data, 97.7% of the 7,158 brake causes of the expert are visible to the ego, and none is an agent ahead
that only the RSU sees ( Sec. 7 ).
A recent closed-loop benchmark also reports that sharing perception does not
always improve planning [ 13 ] .

blocks.en:
We argue that shared information need not enter the planner at all. Two observations support this. First, predicting the future motion of the
surrounding agents from shared detections is densely supervised : the future track of every observed agent in every frame is a
training target [ 6 ] , and an agent that only another source sees is obtained by dropping its ego detection, without a new
expert action. Shared observations have been shown to
improve forecasting [ 54 , 62 , 81 ] . Second, an
ego planner that scores candidate trajectories [ 31 , 38 , 41 , 36 , 43 , 68 ] typically has the kind of response that a decision-making moment demands. Candidates who follow the same path at different speeds cover slowing and
yielding. Recent vocabularies also vary the path: they are factorized into paths and speed
profiles [ 59 ] , and candidates ranked below the executed one can include lateral alternatives such as
lane changes [ 43 ] , so taking a neighboring path is also a candidate. The planner lacks only
the information to prefer one of them. Given predicted futures, we can test in every frame whether each candidate is safe,
and when to react follows from this test. We cast cooperation as selection : the planner proposes, and shared
information decides which candidate from its vocabulary is executed. Selecting among a learned planner’s own candidates with an explicit
safety check has been used for the safety of ego-only planners [ 53 , 31 ] . We make it the only place where
cooperation enters.

We propose CoSel, a cooperative driving system built on this formulation ( Fig. 2 ). Its planner uses
ego-only input, in training and at test time. A cooperative predictor estimates an existence probability and several possible futures for every surrounding agent

CAV shares and the static obstacles that a roadside LiDAR sees. Among
the candidates that satisfy a chance constraint on predicted collision risk with a fixed risk budget, a selector
executes the one closest to the planner’s choice. Only the predictor is trained on cooperative data,
and its targets are the future tracks of all agents.

Cooperation as selection gives CoSel three properties by design, where an intervention is a step at which
the executed candidate differs from the planner’s choice. Planner first : the planner’s choice is executed
unchanged unless the predicted risk rules it out or progress requires a move ( Sec. 3.4 ). One safety rule for every
source : an agent or obstacle enters the chance constraint as one factor of the same form whether the ego, an RSU or
a CAV reported it, and a source that reports nothing contributes no factor and leaves the rule unchanged
( Secs. 3.3 and 4.3 ). Traceable interventions : every safety intervention is attributed to the
agent or obstacle that contributes most to the predicted risk of the planner’s choice, together with the source
that reported it ( Sec. 4.2 ).

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Early work on cooperative driving focused on perception: vehicles and roadside units exchange raw data, intermediate features or
detected objects and fuse them to see beyond occlusion, with datasets [ 71 , 76 , 77 , 72 , 67 , 82 , 22 , 49 ] and fusion schemes that are efficient in bandwidth and robust to delay, pose error and
heterogeneity [ 70 , 24 , 63 , 47 , 26 , 69 , 55 , 27 ] . Later work extended cooperation to
prediction [ 77 , 62 , 79 , 54 , 81 ] and to planning. End-to-end cooperative systems fuse shared features or queries and
then plan, training the whole stack jointly. Most are evaluated in open loop [ 78 , 40 , 57 , 11 ] , while
V2Xverse/CoDriving [ 46 ] closes the loop in CARLA. COOPERNAUT [ 14 ] learns a fused driving policy in
closed loop on scenarios constructed so that the shared view decides the outcome, with corrective demonstrations collected
online. V2Xverse training data rarely contain such moments ( Sec. 7 ). A parallel line shares intents in natural language and negotiates
maneuvers with LLM- or VLM-based agents [ 45 , 20 , 19 , 10 , 2 ] , and closed-loop benchmarks such as
InterDrive [ 45 ] and MDrive [ 13 ] now measure multi-vehicle interaction directly. These works differ in what is shared
and where it enters the stack, but in almost all of them the planner is trained, or prompted, on cooperative input and has to learn from
demonstrations when shared information should change its decision. Shared information
is either always used or gated by learned communication or hand-crafted rules [ 24 , 46 , 45 ] , and its uncertainty
enters at most as a detection confidence or a calibrated score for an LLM decision [ 2 ] . LACO [ 9 ] is, to our knowledge,
the only training-free plug-in. It exchanges latent states between VLA planners, and its effect on individual decisions is not examined.
We instead cast cooperation as selection: the planner uses ego-only input, shared detections feed a densely supervised
predictor, and one chance constraint over the planner’s own candidates decides when shared information changes the decision.

blocks.en:
End-to-end planners map sensors to trajectories, either with a single network that chains perception, prediction and
planning [ 25 , 30 , 65 , 58 ] , with generative decoders [ 43 , 68 , 80 ] , or with world
models that imagine future observations to supervise or evaluate plans [ 61 , 35 , 36 ] . A growing family of
planners separates trajectory generation from selection: they score a fixed or sampled vocabulary of candidates and execute the best
one [ 31 , 38 , 42 , 21 , 74 , 59 ] , mirroring classical planners that rank proposals with hand-crafted or learned
costs [ 16 , 28 ] . Recent work evaluates candidates with world models [ 36 ] or re-ranks the candidates of a
frozen planner [ 44 ] . Rule-based selection among a learned planner’s own candidates [ 53 , 31 ] and safety filters on
learned policies [ 1 ] guard a single vehicle with its own observations. We use selection as the only place
where cooperation enters. Its safety check follows planning under prediction uncertainty, with chance constraints over
multimodal forecasts [ 3 , 50 ] and contingency plans that keep a safe fallback [ 23 , 52 ] . We build on SparseDriveV2 [ 59 ] , which scores a factorized vocabulary of paths and speed profiles and exposes both the
candidates and their scores. CoSel reads both and leaves its network unchanged.

blocks.en: 3 Method
blocks.zh: 3 方法

blocks.en:
Section 1 argued that reacting to shared information takes two things: anticipating how the surrounding agents
will move, and a maneuver that avoids them.
CoSel takes the maneuvers from an ego
planner ( Sec. 3.1 , Fig. 2 a–c) and the futures from a cooperative predictor ( Sec. 3.2 , Fig. 2 d,e), and neither is trained on cooperative demonstrations.
At every decision step, the planner π \pi returns a set of candidate trajectories 𝒞 \mathcal{C} and its choice c π ∈ 𝒞 c_{\pi}\in\mathcal{C} from the ego’s own input.
RSUs send the ego their detections, and other CAVs send their detections, their states and their plans.

It is needed because the predictor’s error grows with the horizon: on the validation towns, its best-mode error averages 0.5 0.5 m over the first 2 s and reaches 2.0 2.0 m at 4 s, more than half a lane width ( Sec. 14 ).
Near an intersection, the modes at the end of the horizon cover much of the road, and a requirement to avoid every
mode rejects most moving candidates.
The chance constraint accepts a candidate that conflicts only with modes of low probability, and the next decision
step tests it again.
We use one δ \delta in all experiments ( Sec. 4.1 ); a smaller δ \delta is more cautious ( Sec. 16 ).

At an unsignalized intersection, the selections of several CAVs are coupled, and two cautious CAVs can wait for each
other indefinitely.
We decompose the joint problem with one shared priority order, as in prioritized planning [ 4 ] ,
and let the order act through the scene.
Two CAVs are in conflict when their paths ahead come closer than a radius r c r_{c} and one does not follow the other; the conflict zone of the CAV with priority is a 6.9 m by 4 m box on its path where the two paths meet.
A lower-priority CAV adds this zone, as an obstacle,
to its scene with e i = 1 e_{i}=1 and a stationary mode until that CAV has passed, as in reservation-based intersection
management [ 18 ] .
Yielding is then one more factor of Eq. 4 , and I2V and V2V cooperation share one mechanism.
To derive the order, CAVs also share their upcoming navigation points, which give each CAV’s path ahead up to D D and
show a turn before the CAV starts to make it.
All CAVs derive the same total order from the shared states, with the earlier estimated arrival at the conflict first
and ties broken by the CAV index, and the order of a pair is fixed while their conflict lasts, unless the CAV with
priority cannot move within a time-out T exp T_{\text{exp}} or has arrived ( Sec. 11 ).
A yielding CAV that is stationary and has no candidate in 𝒢 \mathcal{G} stays stationary.
We assume that CAV states arrive at every decision step and do not study message delay
or loss.

in [ 46 ] , and DS and success rate (SR) on MDrive, as in [ 13 ] .

confidence interval over pairs or scenarios. Every method is run once.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en: We presented CoSel, which casts cooperative driving as selection rather than planner retraining. An ego planner proposes candidate trajectories from ego-only input, while information shared by RSUs and CAVs is used to predict the surrounding scene and determine which candidate should be executed. CoSel preserves the planner’s choice when it remains safe and selects the closest safe alternative when shared information reveals additional risk. This separation allows cooperation to benefit from densely supervised prediction without requiring the planner to learn from rare cooperative decision-changing demonstrations.
blocks.zh: 我们介绍了CoSel, 它将合作驾驶作为选择而不是规划者再培训。 一个自负计划者从自负独有的输入中提出候选人的轨迹,而RSUs和CAVs共享的信息则被用来预测周围的场景,并确定哪些候选人应当被处决. CoSel 保留了规划者的安全选择, 并选择最接近的安全选择, 这种分离使得合作能够从严密监督的预测中受益,而不需要规划者从罕见的合作改变决定的演示中学习.

blocks.en: Without retraining the underlying planner, CoSel achieves the highest driving scores among the compared methods on both V2Xverse and MDrive. It also remains robust when ego detections are removed, with only a small increase in collisions as shared information becomes the primary evidence of otherwise unseen hazards. These results demonstrate that shared information does not need to be fused into a learned driving policy to improve cooperative driving. Instead, cooperation can complement an existing planner by deciding when to keep its choice and when to select another of its maneuvers. CoSel has three limitations that define our next steps. First, it has not yet been tested with other state-of-the-art planners, such as DrivoR [ 32 ] , which run on different platforms. Second, its risk treats agents as independent and its predictor reads only detections, so we will study predictors of the joint future of interacting agents that also include traffic lights. Third, it assumes ideal communication; message delay, pose error, and real-world V2X data remain to be tested.
blocks.zh: 科塞尔在不重新培训基本规划者的情况下,在V2Xverse和MDrive的比较方法中取得了最高的驾驶分数。 当自我发现被移除时,它也依然很强大,只有小幅地增加相撞,因为共享的信息成为其他看不见的危险的主要证据。 这些结果表明,共享的信息不需要融入一项有知识的驱动政策,以改善合作驾驶。 相反,合作可以通过决定何时保持其选择,何时选择其另一种做法来补充现有的规划者。 CoSel有三个限制 来决定我们下一步的步骤 其一,尚未与DrivoR [32]等在不同的平台上运行的其他最先进的规划者进行测试. 第二,它的风险将物剂视为独立的,它的预测器只读出检测结果,因此我们将研究互动物剂的共同未来的预测器,其中也包括交通灯. 第三,它假设理想的通信;消息延迟,形成错误,而现实世界的V2X数据仍然有待测试.

explains the expert’s action. We count such frames in V2Xverse training data. We collected these data with the routes and the spawn positions of the data-collection scripts that

The data cover 167 routes in CARLA 0.9.10, each driven by two ego vehicles under the V2Xverse expert, with road-side units placed as in
V2Xverse (one per ego, re-placed ahead of it as it drives), saved at 5 Hz. For 18 routes the ego’s front segmentation is missing, so its

An agent is visible to the ego if at least four corners of its 3D box are visible in the semantic segmentation of the ego’s front, left and

visible to an RSU. It is sustained if the expert brakes for the agent for at least 1 s and the agent is visible only to the RSU in at
least three of those frames. Events whose cause is the other ego vehicle are not counted as RSU-decisive.

blocks.en:
The stress test is a hard diagnostic set that we built so that cooperative information is decisive. Each of its 72 short scenarios is staged next to a fixed RSU rig (four 100 ∘ 100^{\circ} cameras, pitch − 40 ∘ -40^{\circ} , 7.5 m high) that covers the conflict area: in 40 scenarios (R1) a pedestrian (adult, child, elderly or jogger) steps out from behind a kiosk, a parked truck or a van, 1.4–5.0 s before reaching the ego’s path, in clear, rainy or sunset light; in 5 (R2) a vehicle enters a junction from behind an occluder; 3 lane-change conflicts (R4), and 24 controls (R5): 8 with a crossing that the ego sees, 8 with a pedestrian who walks
away along the sidewalk and never enters the road, and 8 without a pedestrian. When a pedestrian starts to walk toward the ego’s path, the ego is a median of 12 m from the crossing point in the stress test, against 35 m on V2Xverse-85 and 20 m on MDrive. In the setting used for the analysis in Sec. 4.3 , the pedestrians are additionally removed from the ego’s cameras and LiDAR, so that the RSU is the only evidence about them: without the RSU boxes, the planner alone and our selection on ego evidence collide in 39 and 38 of the 40 dart-outs. The set is used only to diagnose the cooperative channel; no parameter is chosen on it. Remaining collisions. With full ego sensing CoSel collides in 17 scenarios, 13 with a pedestrian and 4 with a vehicle.
The 40 step-out scenarios differ in the time between the moment the pedestrian becomes visible to the ego and its entry into the ego’s lane:
in 18 it is 1.0–1.5 s (median 1.0 s), in 22 it is 1.8–2.7 s. A full stop from the approach speed of 5 m/s takes 1.1 s with a reaction time
of 0.3 s and a deceleration of 6 m/s 2 . Nine of the 11 step-out collisions of CoSel fall in the first group and 2 in the second.
In 14 of the 17 collisions the planner’s choice had exceeded the risk budget within the 3 s before the contact, so the selector had acted.
The pedestrians follow a scripted motion and do not react to the ego: in 9 of the 13 pedestrian collisions the pedestrian meets the right
side of the moving ego, and in 4 the front of the ego after it has braked to below 0.5 m/s.

Each detected box of the present and the three previous decision steps (0.6 s) is a token with its position, heading, size, class, score,
source, age and velocity, in the present ego frame; a plan of a CAV over 2 s is one more token.
All CAVs decide at the same step, so the newest plan of a CAV is the candidate that it chose at the previous step and is executing;
the ego places this candidate at the CAV’s present pose.
Only a plan that ends in a stop is taken as given: the CAV can always brake, so it goes no farther than the end of such a plan, and if
other agents hold it up, it stops earlier on the same path, which its next message shows.
We take such a message as given instead of predicting the CAV for three reasons.
The predictor gives each agent a marginal future and would spread probability over futures that the CAV has already ruled out by its
own decision; a stationary CAV or a stop plan fixes the CAV over the whole horizon H H by the CAV’s own action alone, so the ego can
plan around it as around a static obstacle; and the message is replaced at the next decision step, so the assumption lasts one step.
The interaction between CAVs, which this does not model, enters through their shared order and the conflict zones of Sec. 3.4 ; a plan that ends in motion depends on that interaction and stays an input of the predictor.
Three self-attention layers of width 128 (0.53 M parameters) output, for every present box, M = 6 M=6 trajectories over H = 4 H=4 s in steps of
0.2 s as offsets from constant velocity, their probabilities and the existence e i e_{i} .

weighted 0.5.
Training removes the ego’s boxes of an agent that another source also sees with probability 0.5, all RSU boxes with 0.2 and all CAV boxes
and plans with 0.3; a plan is given with probability 0.5.
We train four epochs on 63k frames from Towns 1–4 and 6 with AdamW (learning rate 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} , batch size 32); Towns 7 and 10 are
used for validation.

We fused the RSU detections into the planner in two ways: through a cooperative perception head whose fused queries the planner
reads, and as additional tokens of the planner’s agent attention. Frozen planner. With the fused queries, the average displacement error on 10,208 held-out frames falls by 0.026 m [ 0.020 , 0.032 ] [0.020,0.032] , but the planner slows less often when the expert brakes ( − 4.8 -4.8 points [ − 6.8 , − 3.0 ] [-6.8,-3.0] ).
With the additional tokens, the speed of the planner’s choice changes as much with the RSU tokens of another frame as with the real
ones (paired difference − 0.005 -0.005 m/s). Adapter. A 131 k-parameter adapter on the RSU tokens, trained on the full training set with the planner frozen, slows the
planner wherever tokens are present; trained on real tokens or on shuffled tokens it behaves the same on the frames in which the RSU
sees the cause of the expert’s braking (paired difference of the chosen speed − 0.028 -0.028 m/s [ − 0.102 , + 0.037 ] [-0.102,+0.037] ). Joint training. A planner fine-tuned on ten routes with the fused queries is not better than one fine-tuned without them and
given them only at test time (displacement error 0.696 m against 0.682 m), and on the 93 frames in which only the RSU sees the
cause of the expert’s braking it slows in 38% with the RSU and 42% without. Closed loop. On V2Xverse-85 the planner trained with fused RSU features does not improve on the same planner without them
(paired DS difference − 6.7 -6.7 [ − 13.0 , − 0.1 ] [-13.0,-0.1] ); the two also differ in their training schedule. Why. The expert data of this benchmark explain this: with the RSU 12 m ahead of the ego, among the 7,158 braking events of the expert there is no sustained one whose cause is an
agent ahead that only the RSU sees ( Sec. 7 ), so no training sample requires the fused features, and shuffling them at test time changes the planned speed by 0.005 m/s.
Fusion can learn such a response from data constructed to contain it [ 14 ] ; selection does not depend on such data.

blocks.en:
We trained a scorer that reads the candidates of the frozen planner and the detected boxes and predicts a contact within 2 s, on all
119,857 frames of the training set.
Its AUROC on held-out frames is 0.945, and 0.958 with the velocity of the tracked boxes as input.
On 19 closed-loop collisions with a pedestrian that steps into the lane, it flags the planner’s choice one to two seconds before the
impact in 1 case from the boxes alone and in 9 with RSU boxes and their velocity.
Re-ranking the final candidates avoids 1 of the 19: in 18, the planner had removed every safe speed profile in its first scoring
round.
A hard veto in that first round removed candidates at 49% of the decision steps in closed loop, and the route completion fell from
93.6 to 74.5 on the first six routes, where we stopped the run.
The comparison shows that the candidates that reach the selection matter: the scorer worked on the final candidates, from which the safe
speed profiles were already gone. The candidates of CoSel therefore come from before the planner’s final round and always include the stop
profile. The comparison does not show whether predicting the motion of the agents is better than predicting the contact of a candidate.

blocks.en:
The risk budget 0.3 was chosen on 53 validation scenarios in Town10 (32) and Town07 (21), none of them in Town05. Table 8 repeats the scan with the selector of this paper: the planner-alone run of these scenarios is replayed offline, and at each of
its 8,338 decision steps the selector chooses from the logged state.
A step is unsafe when the executed candidate, followed over H H , touches the logged future of an agent; with the planner’s own choice 8.70% of the
steps are unsafe.
The table also gives how many of the 11 scenarios in which the planner alone has a contact are flagged before the contact, how early, and how often the six
scenarios without a conflict are flagged.
The budget trades the unsafe steps against the flags on scenarios without a conflict, without a knee. Other constants. On the same scenarios we varied nine constants of the selector one at a time: the deceleration of the stop continuation
(2 and 4 m/s 2 ), the reaction time (0.3 and 1 s) and the deceleration of the other agents, the radius of the ego footprint ( ± 0.1 \pm 0.1 m), the margin on
standing agents, the number of candidate paths (8 and 32), the acceleration bound of the committed prefix, the standing threshold (0.3 and 0.8 m/s) and T stall T_{\text{stall}} (2 and 8 s).
For the first seven the executed candidate changes at no more than 1.2% of the steps and the unsafe steps stay between 7.77% and 7.81%.
The standing threshold and T stall T_{\text{stall}} change how often the selector moves a standing ego on, and the unsafe steps stay between 7.65% and 7.78%.
The replay is open loop; the start corridor, the lane lines, the static obstacles and the order between CAVs have no input on these scenarios.
On V2Xverse-85 the planner’s choice has a predicted risk of exactly zero at 63% of the decision steps and above 0.3 at 21%. Collisions within the budget. A budget of 0.3 accepts candidates with a predicted risk up to 0.3, and we count the collisions that it let pass.
For every collision of CoSel with an agent we take the decision steps of the 3 s before the impact.
On V2Xverse-85 the planner’s choice exceeds the budget at one of these steps in 27 of the 31 collisions, so the selector had already acted; in 4 the predicted risk
stays within the budget (at most 0.24), 3 of them with the ego driving into a pedestrian; in none is it zero.
On the stress test with the pedestrians masked the counts are 11, 3 and 5 of 19.
The risk is that of the whole scene, so 4 and 3 are upper bounds of the collisions that a smaller budget could have changed.
